text: This is the payoff for the whole chapter. Everything about eigenvalues and eigenvectors you've built up comes together in one of the strangest and most important facts in quantum computing: when you measure a qubit, the only possible outcomes are the eigenvalues of the thing you're measuring, and the state jumps to the matching eigenvector.

A measurable physical quantity is represented by an observable — a Hermitian operator, whose eigenvalues are always real, since a measurement has to produce a real, readable number. The measurement postulate says two things: the result is always one of the observable's eigenvalues, never any other number, and immediately afterward the qubit's state collapses to the eigenvector matching whichever eigenvalue came out.

Pauli-Z has eigenvalues plus one and minus one, with eigenvectors ket-zero and ket-one. Measuring Z can only ever return plus one or minus one — never any other value. If the result is plus one, the state collapses to ket-zero; if it's minus one, it collapses to ket-one. That's the mathematical reason a qubit measurement is binary.

Take a qubit in superposition, 3 fifths ket-zero plus 4 fifths ket-one — already confirmed normalized, since 3 fifths squared plus 4 fifths squared equals 1. Measuring Z can only return plus one or minus one, and the probability of each is the squared amplitude on the matching eigenvector: 9 twenty-fifths, or 0.36, for plus one, and 16 twenty-fifths, or 0.64, for minus one — summing to exactly 1, as required.

Classically, measuring just reveals a value that was already there. Quantum measurement is different: before you measure, the qubit genuinely has no definite value of Z — it's a combination of both eigenvectors. The act of measuring forces one specific eigenvalue out, with a probability set by the amplitudes, and changes the state itself in the process. None of that is extra mysticism — it's linear algebra, applied to a physical act.
